J. L. Austin is called a naive empiricist because his ordinary-language method treats “what we should say when,” collected by case-by-case fieldwork, as philosophy’s basic evidence. He held that cataloguing those linguistic distinctions would dissolve traditional problems, the approach of *A Plea for Excuses*, *Sense and Sensibilia*, and *How to Do Things with Words*. “Naive” marks the assumption that ordinary usage is straightforward, theory-neutral data and that description alone can settle the questions.

CONFIDENCE: 74
